about: Synthetic benchmark F: year-end reliability and maintenance review of a fictional metro network's station and line-side assets. 9 domain_method defects, 3 control defects (causal_claim, denominator, overclaim), 11 decoys, 4 plain paragraphs. All arithmetic is exact; no arithmetic or unsourced-figure defects are planted.

why.P04: Components in series: system reliability is the product of component reliabilities (0.98 x 0.96 x 0.99 = 93.1%), not their average (97.7%); the section actually misses the 97.0% target.
why.P05: Mean time to repair here is active repair only; restoration time seen by passengers must add response (1.6 h) and spares waiting (0.9 h), giving 4.9 h, so the 3-hour promise and the 99.92% availability are both overstated (correct 99.84%).
why.P07: Battery capacity loss is a hidden failure that float-voltage and temperature alarms do not reveal; zero alarms says nothing about whether the batteries would support load, and withdrawing the discharge (failure-finding) test leaves the hidden failure undetected.
why.P08: The q-squared calculation assumes independence, but both pumps depend on one shared level controller; the common-cause term dominates (0.5% controller unavailability gives about 0.54% sump unavailability, over ten times the stated 0.04%).
why.P10: The condition-monitoring interval must be well inside the P-F interval (typically no more than half of it); a 13-week survey against an 8-week P-F interval will miss most developing gearbox failures.
why.P12: A Weibull shape parameter well above 1 (3.4) indicates wear-out with an increasing hazard rate, not random failure; age-based replacement can be effective and should be evaluated against cost.
why.P14: The backlog target is met by deferring safety-critical corrective work (PSD obstruction-detection sensors protect passengers from being trapped) for most of a year; safety-critical defects must be prioritised by risk, not moved to meet a KPI.
why.P16: Criticality must weigh consequence (safety, service impact) and likelihood, not cost alone; track circuits are cheap to repair but each failure stops train detection and disrupts the line, so ranking by corrective cost misdirects the budget.
why.P17: MTBF from a fleet's constant-hazard period is a failure rate, not a service life; a 41.2-year MTBF says nothing about when wear-out begins, so it cannot justify extending the renewal horizon to 40 years.
why.P18: A one-year before/after fall is attributed to the contractor without controlling for other causes (regression to the mean, demand, asset renewals, recording changes); the contract decision rests on an untested causal claim.
why.P19: The failure rate per pump uses sumps (37) as the denominator instead of pumps (74); the correct rate is 29.7% per pump-year, below the 35% benchmark.
why.P20: Zero failures in six sections over five months is a tiny sample (about six failures expected at the old rate) and cannot show the design eliminates failures; it does not justify a AED 43.7 million fleet-wide renewal.
why.P03: Excluding planned work done in engineering hours is correct for a passenger-facing availability measured over the service window; downtime inside the service window, planned and unplanned, is counted.
why.P06: Twin of P05 done right: restoration time includes response, repair and waiting for parts, and it reconciles to the unplanned downtime in P03.
why.P09: Twin of P08 done right: the rectifiers have separate transformers, protection, feeders from different bulk supply points and no shared control, so the independence assumption behind q-squared is justified.
why.P11: Twin of P10 done right: extending to fortnightly still keeps the review interval at or below half of the 6-week P-F interval.
why.P13: Correct reading of a shape parameter below 1 (infant mortality): age-based replacement would add failures, and supplier burn-in is the right response.
why.P15: Correct run-to-failure: decorative fittings have no safety or operational function, failures are evident, emergency lighting is a separate tested system, and the cost case holds.
why.P21: Correct exposure-based comparison: because duty (running hours) differs between groups, failures per running hour is the right basis, and it reverses the per-unit ranking.
why.P22: Correct PM compliance: completion within a tolerance window of the scheduled interval, with the old any-time basis disclosed for comparison; the lower figure is the honest one.
why.P23: Correct spares sizing: stock set from the Poisson distribution of lead-time demand to a stated service level, not from the average demand.
why.P24: Correct: the contract target is defined as a median, so testing the median against it is the right comparison.
why.P25: Correct: monitoring effectiveness is judged on confirmation rate and detection of failures before they occur, not on the count of alarms.
